lessons.title: Line, Shape, and Form
lessons.content: Line is the most basic element of art — a mark moving through space. Lines can be straight, curved, thick, thin, broken, or continuous. They create direction, movement, and emotion: horizontal lines feel calm, vertical lines feel strong, diagonal lines feel dynamic, and zigzag lines feel energetic. Shapes are two-dimensional (flat): geometric (circles, squares, triangles) or organic (irregular, natural). Forms are three-dimensional shapes: spheres, cubes, cones. Artists use shading (light and shadow) to make flat shapes look like 3D forms. Everything you draw starts with basic shapes — a human figure is circles, rectangles, and triangles combined.
examples: A tree: trunk is a rectangle, canopy is an irregular organic shape, branches are curved lines
Shading a circle to look like a sphere: light side, gradual transition, dark side, cast shadow
Picasso simplified faces into geometric shapes — demonstrating that art can abstract reality

keyTerms.line: A mark moving through space — the most fundamental element of art
keyTerms.shape: A two-dimensional enclosed area — geometric (circle, square) or organic (irregular)
keyTerms.form: A three-dimensional object with length, width, and depth (sphere, cube, cone)

quiz.question: What is the difference between shape and form?
quiz.explanation: Shapes are flat (circle), forms have depth (sphere) — shading creates the illusion of form.

quiz.question: Diagonal lines create a feeling of:
quiz.explanation: Diagonal lines feel dynamic and full of motion — unlike stable horizontal or vertical lines.

quiz.question: How do artists make shapes look 3D?
quiz.explanation: Shading creates the illusion of depth — light and dark areas make flat shapes look like 3D forms.

lessons.title: Color Theory
lessons.content: Color is the most powerful visual element. Primary colors (red, blue, yellow) cannot be made by mixing. Secondary colors are made by mixing two primaries: red + blue = purple, red + yellow = orange, blue + yellow = green. Tertiary colors mix a primary with an adjacent secondary. The color wheel organizes all colors. Complementary colors are opposite on the wheel (red-green, blue-orange) — they create strong contrast. Analogous colors are next to each other (blue, blue-green, green) — they create harmony. Color has three properties: hue (the color name), value (lightness/darkness — add white for tint, black for shade), and saturation (intensity — vivid vs. dull).
examples: Complementary contrast: a red flower against green leaves stands out dramatically
A sunset uses analogous warm colors: red, orange, yellow — creating natural harmony
Adding white to red creates pink (a tint); adding black creates maroon (a shade)

keyTerms.primary colors: Red, blue, yellow — colors that cannot be created by mixing other colors
keyTerms.complementary colors: Colors opposite each other on the color wheel — create maximum contrast
keyTerms.value: The lightness or darkness of a color — tints (add white), shades (add black)

quiz.question: What are the primary colors?
quiz.explanation: In traditional color theory, red, blue, and yellow are the three primary colors.

quiz.question: Red and green are:
quiz.explanation: Red and green are opposite on the color wheel — they're complementary.

quiz.question: Adding white to a color creates:
quiz.explanation: White + color = tint. Black + color = shade.

lessons.title: Texture, Space, and Composition
lessons.content: Texture is how a surface feels or looks like it feels. Actual texture: you can touch it (rough bark, smooth glass). Visual texture: created by artists to look textured (painted brick wall). Space is the area within and around objects. Positive space is the subject; negative space is the empty area around it. Perspective creates the illusion of depth on a flat surface: objects appear smaller as they get farther away, and parallel lines converge at a vanishing point. Composition is how elements are arranged in an artwork. The Rule of Thirds places the subject at intersection points of a 3×3 grid — more interesting than centering everything.
examples: Visual texture: Van Gogh's thick brushstrokes make his paintings look textured from across the room
Negative space: the FedEx logo has an arrow hidden in the negative space between E and x
Rule of Thirds: in a landscape photo, place the horizon on the top or bottom third line, not the middle

keyTerms.texture: The surface quality of an artwork — how it feels or appears to feel
keyTerms.negative space: The empty area around and between subjects in an artwork
keyTerms.composition: The arrangement of visual elements within an artwork

quiz.question: Negative space is:
options: The empty area around the subject
quiz.explanation: Negative space is the background/empty area — positive space is the subject itself.

quiz.question: The Rule of Thirds suggests:
options: Place subjects at intersection points of a 3×3 grid
quiz.explanation: Off-center placement creates more dynamic, interesting compositions.

quiz.question: How do artists create depth on a flat surface?
options: Perspective — objects get smaller in the distance
quiz.explanation: Perspective: smaller objects appear farther away, lines converge at vanishing points.

lessons.title: Drawing Fundamentals
lessons.content: Drawing is the foundation of all visual art. Start with gesture drawing — quick sketches (30-60 seconds) to capture movement and proportion. Use basic shapes to build complex subjects: circles for heads, rectangles for torsos. Pencil grades: H pencils are hard and light (for fine lines), B pencils are soft and dark (for shading). Shading techniques: hatching (parallel lines), cross-hatching (overlapping lines), stippling (dots), and blending (smooth gradients). Practice contour drawing (following edges without looking at your paper) to improve hand-eye coordination. Draw daily — even 10 minutes improves skill dramatically.
examples: Gesture drawing: 30-second sketches of people walking capture movement and energy
Cross-hatching: closely spaced crossing lines create darker areas — wider spacing for lighter areas
Drawing a face: start with an oval, horizontal line for eyes (at the midpoint), nose at 3/4 down, mouth at 7/8

keyTerms.gesture drawing: Quick sketches (30-60 seconds) capturing the movement and essence of a subject
keyTerms.hatching: Creating tone by drawing parallel lines — closer lines = darker value
keyTerms.contour drawing: Drawing the outline/edges of a subject, focusing on what you see

quiz.question: What is gesture drawing?
options: Quick sketches capturing movement and energy
quiz.explanation: Gesture drawings are rapid (30-60 seconds) to capture the essence and movement of a subject.

quiz.question: B pencils are:
options: Soft and dark — good for shading
quiz.explanation: B = bold/soft. Higher B numbers (6B) are darker. H pencils are hard and light.

quiz.question: The best way to improve at drawing is:
quiz.explanation: Consistent practice is the key to improvement — skill builds with repetition.

lessons.title: Painting Basics
lessons.content: Painting adds color to drawing. Main paint types: watercolor (transparent, mixes on wet paper, hard to correct), acrylic (versatile, dries fast, can layer), and oil (rich colors, slow drying, blendable). Color mixing is essential: know your color wheel and mix from primaries rather than buying every color. Start with an underpainting (basic tones), then layer: background first, then midground, then foreground and details. Brush techniques: flat brush for broad areas, round brush for details, dry brush for texture. Let layers dry between applications for clean colors. Clean brushes immediately after use — dried paint ruins them.
examples: Watercolor: wet the paper first, then add paint — colors flow and blend beautifully but unpredictably
Acrylic layers: paint the sky first, let dry, then paint trees on top — clean edges
Color mixing: you only NEED red, blue, yellow, white, and black — mix everything else

keyTerms.watercolor: A transparent paint that uses water as a medium — known for soft, flowing effects
keyTerms.acrylic: A versatile, fast-drying paint that can mimic watercolor or oil techniques
keyTerms.underpainting: A base layer of paint establishing basic tones and composition before adding details

quiz.question: Which paint type dries the fastest?
options: All dry at the same speed
quiz.explanation: Acrylic dries in minutes. Oil paint can take days or weeks to dry fully.

quiz.question: What three paint colors can you mix everything from?
quiz.explanation: The three primaries plus white and black can create any color through mixing.

quiz.question: Why paint background before foreground?
options: So foreground objects sit on top with clean edges
quiz.explanation: Painting back to front means closer objects overlap farther ones — creating natural depth.

lessons.title: Sculpture and 3D Art
lessons.content: Sculpture is three-dimensional art. Techniques: carving (removing material — stone, wood), modeling (adding material — clay, wax), casting (pouring liquid into a mold — bronze, plaster), and assembling (joining pieces — welded metal, found objects). Clay is the most accessible medium — air-dry clay needs no kiln. Consider all viewing angles — sculpture is seen from 360°, unlike a painting. Relief sculpture is raised from a flat background (like coins). Freestanding sculpture stands independently. Modern sculpture includes installations (art that fills a space), kinetic sculpture (moving parts), and environmental art (using natural materials in nature).
examples: Michelangelo carved David from a single block of marble — removing everything that wasn't David
Clay coil pot: roll clay into coils, stack and smooth them to build a vessel
Alexander Calder invented mobiles — hanging kinetic sculptures that move with air currents

keyTerms.carving: A subtractive sculpture technique — removing material to reveal form
keyTerms.modeling: An additive sculpture technique — building up material (clay, wax) to create form
keyTerms.installation: An artwork designed to transform a space — the viewer enters or walks through it

quiz.question: Carving is a:
quiz.explanation: Carving removes material (cutting away stone or wood) to reveal the form.

quiz.question: What makes sculpture different from painting?
options: Sculpture is three-dimensional — viewable from all angles
quiz.explanation: Sculpture has depth and can be viewed from 360° — paintings are flat (2D).

quiz.question: Which material is easiest for beginners?
quiz.explanation: Air-dry clay is affordable, forgiving, and hardens without a kiln.

lessons.title: Ancient and Classical Art
lessons.content: Art is as old as humanity. Cave paintings (Lascaux, 17,000 years ago) depict animals and hunting scenes — the first known art. Egyptian art followed strict rules: figures shown from the side, important people drawn larger. Greek art pursued idealized human beauty: realistic sculptures with perfect proportions. Roman art was practical: mosaics, architecture, and portrait sculptures capturing real faces (not idealized). African art has ancient traditions: Nok terracotta sculptures (Nigeria, 500 BCE), Benin Bronzes (sophisticated casting), and rock art across the continent. Art served religion, recording history, and expressing cultural identity.
examples: Lascaux cave paintings: artists used natural pigments (charcoal, iron oxide) and blew paint through hollow bones
Greek Parthenon sculptures: idealized human forms representing gods and athletes
Benin Bronzes: incredibly detailed bronze plaques from the Kingdom of Benin (1400-1897) — among the finest metalwork ever made

keyTerms.cave painting: Prehistoric art on cave walls — the earliest known human artistic expression
keyTerms.idealized: Representing subjects as perfect or ideal rather than realistic
keyTerms.Benin Bronzes: Elaborate bronze sculptures from the Kingdom of Benin in present-day Nigeria

quiz.question: The oldest known artworks are:
options: Cave paintings (tens of thousands of years old)
quiz.explanation: Cave paintings like those at Lascaux (~17,000 years old) are the earliest known art.

quiz.question: Greek art focused on:
options: Idealized human beauty and perfect proportions
quiz.explanation: Greek artists pursued ideal beauty — perfectly proportioned human figures.

quiz.question: Benin Bronzes demonstrate:
options: Sophisticated metalwork from the Kingdom of Benin
quiz.explanation: These intricate bronze works show the advanced artistry of the Benin Kingdom.

lessons.title: Renaissance to Impressionism
lessons.content: The Renaissance (1400-1600) revolutionized European art with perspective (3D depth on flat surfaces), realistic anatomy, and oil painting. Masters: Leonardo da Vinci (Mona Lisa), Michelangelo (Sistine Chapel), Raphael (School of Athens). Baroque (1600-1750) added drama, emotion, and movement (Caravaggio, Rembrandt). Romanticism (1800s) celebrated nature, emotion, and individual expression (Turner, Delacroix). Impressionism (1860s-1880s) broke from tradition: loose brushstrokes, light effects, everyday scenes painted outdoors. Monet, Renoir, and Degas captured moments rather than perfect details — revolutionary at the time.
examples: Leonardo's Mona Lisa: mysterious smile, sfumato technique (smoky blending), revolutionary portrait
Monet's Water Lilies: painted the same pond hundreds of times at different times of day — capturing changing light
Caravaggio used dramatic lighting (chiaroscuro) — deep shadows and bright highlights for theatrical effect

keyTerms.Renaissance art: European art movement (1400-1600) emphasizing realism, perspective, and human beauty
keyTerms.Impressionism: Art movement (1860s-1880s) using loose brushstrokes to capture light and momentary effects
keyTerms.chiaroscuro: Strong contrast between light and dark to create dramatic effect

quiz.question: Impressionism is characterized by:
options: Loose brushstrokes capturing light and moments
quiz.explanation: Impressionists painted quickly with visible brushstrokes to capture fleeting light effects.

quiz.question: Who painted the Mona Lisa?
quiz.explanation: Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa around 1503-1519.

quiz.question: The Renaissance introduced what technique for showing depth?
quiz.explanation: Linear perspective uses vanishing points to create realistic 3D depth on a flat surface.

lessons.title: Modern and Contemporary Art
lessons.content: Modern art (1880s-1970s) broke all traditional rules. Post-Impressionism (Van Gogh, Cézanne) emphasized emotion and structure. Cubism (Picasso, Braque) showed multiple viewpoints simultaneously. Surrealism (Dalí, Magritte) explored dreams and the subconscious. Abstract art (Kandinsky, Mondrian) abandoned representation entirely — using color, line, and form for their own sake. Pop Art (Warhol, Lichtenstein) celebrated popular culture and consumerism. Contemporary art (1970s-present) includes everything: installations, performance, video, digital art, and street art (Banksy). Art today questions what art even is — anything can be art if it communicates meaning.
examples: Picasso's Guernica: cubist painting showing the horrors of war — multiple perspectives in one image
Warhol's Campbell's Soup Cans: pop art questioning the boundary between art and commercial products
Banksy: anonymous street artist whose works combine humor, political commentary, and public accessibility

keyTerms.abstract art: Art that doesn't represent real objects — uses color, form, and line for their own sake
keyTerms.cubism: Art showing multiple viewpoints of a subject simultaneously — invented by Picasso and Braque
keyTerms.contemporary art: Art from the 1970s to present — encompasses all media and often challenges traditional definitions

quiz.question: Cubism shows subjects:
quiz.explanation: Cubism fragments subjects and reassembles them from multiple perspectives at once.

quiz.question: Abstract art:
options: Doesn't represent real objects — uses form and color for expression
quiz.explanation: Abstract art communicates through visual elements themselves, not by depicting reality.

quiz.question: Pop Art celebrated:
options: Popular culture and everyday consumer products
quiz.explanation: Pop artists like Warhol elevated everyday objects (soup cans, celebrities) to fine art.

lessons.title: Graphic Design
lessons.content: Graphic design communicates messages visually. It combines typography (fonts), images, colors, and layout to create logos, posters, websites, packaging, and social media content. Principles: hierarchy (most important info stands out), contrast (differences that draw attention), alignment (organized placement), repetition (consistent style), and whitespace (empty space that lets designs breathe). Typography matters: serif fonts (Times) feel traditional, sans-serif (Arial) feel modern, display fonts are decorative. A professional designer considers the audience, purpose, and medium. Tools: Canva (beginner), Adobe Illustrator and Photoshop (professional).
examples: A poster: large bold title (hierarchy), contrasting colors (contrast), consistent font style (repetition)
Apple's branding: clean sans-serif font, lots of whitespace, minimal color — feels modern and premium
A restaurant menu: serif font for the name (elegant), clear sections, appetizing food photos

keyTerms.typography: The art of selecting and arranging fonts/typefaces for readability and visual appeal
keyTerms.hierarchy: Organizing visual elements so the most important information stands out first
keyTerms.whitespace: Empty space in a design that gives elements room to breathe

quiz.question: Visual hierarchy means:
options: The most important information stands out first
quiz.explanation: Hierarchy guides the viewer's eye to what matters most — through size, color, and position.

quiz.question: Serif fonts are associated with:
quiz.explanation: Serif fonts (like Times New Roman) have small strokes on letter edges — feeling classic and formal.

quiz.question: Why is whitespace important?
options: It gives elements room to breathe and improves readability
quiz.explanation: Whitespace reduces clutter, improves focus, and makes designs more elegant and readable.

lessons.title: Photography Basics
lessons.content: Photography captures light to create images. Three key camera settings: aperture (how wide the lens opens — controls depth of field: wide aperture blurs background, narrow keeps everything sharp), shutter speed (how long the sensor is exposed — fast freezes motion, slow creates blur), and ISO (sensor sensitivity — higher ISO for dark conditions but adds grain/noise). Composition rules: Rule of Thirds, leading lines (roads, fences guiding the eye), framing (using doorways or branches to frame the subject), and symmetry. Golden hour (shortly after sunrise or before sunset) provides the most beautiful, warm light. Smartphones have made photography accessible to everyone.
examples: Portrait mode on phones simulates wide aperture — blurring the background to focus on the person
A waterfall with slow shutter speed (1/4 second) creates a silky water effect
Leading lines: a road disappearing into the distance draws the viewer's eye through the photo

keyTerms.aperture: The lens opening size — controls how much light enters and depth of field
keyTerms.shutter speed: How long the camera sensor is exposed to light — controls motion blur
keyTerms.golden hour: The time shortly after sunrise or before sunset when light is warm and soft

quiz.question: To blur the background in a portrait, use:
quiz.explanation: Wide aperture (f/1.8, f/2.8) creates shallow depth of field — background blurs.

quiz.question: To freeze fast motion (sports), use:
quiz.explanation: Fast shutter speed (1/500s or faster) captures a split second, freezing movement.

quiz.question: Golden hour is special because:
options: The light is warm, soft, and flattering
It's the hottest time of day
quiz.explanation: Low-angle sunlight creates warm tones and soft shadows — ideal for photography.

lessons.title: Art in Everyday Life
lessons.content: Art is not just in museums — it shapes our daily environment. Architecture designs the buildings we live and work in — form and function combined. Interior design creates comfortable, beautiful spaces. Fashion design is wearable art — expressing identity through clothing. Product design makes everyday objects (phones, chairs, packaging) both functional and attractive. Urban art (murals, sculptures in public spaces) makes cities more vibrant and culturally rich. Art therapy uses creative expression to improve mental health. Understanding art helps you appreciate beauty, think creatively, and communicate visually — skills valuable in every career.
examples: The Sydney Opera House: architecture as iconic art — its sail-shaped roof is recognized worldwide
A well-designed chair (like Eames Lounge Chair) is both comfortable to sit in and beautiful to look at
Hospital murals: art on walls reduces patient anxiety and speeds recovery — proven by medical research

keyTerms.applied art: Art with a practical function — architecture, fashion, product, and graphic design
keyTerms.architecture: The art and science of designing buildings and spaces
keyTerms.art therapy: Using creative expression to improve mental health and emotional wellbeing

quiz.question: Applied art is:
options: Art with a practical function (architecture, design, fashion)
quiz.explanation: Applied arts combine aesthetic beauty with practical function — design for daily life.

quiz.question: How does art benefit everyday life?
options: It makes spaces beautiful, products functional, and improves wellbeing
Only rich people benefit from art
quiz.explanation: Art shapes our environment, products, communication, and mental health every day.

quiz.question: Art therapy works by:
options: Using creative expression to improve mental health
quiz.explanation: Creating art can reduce stress, process emotions, and improve wellbeing — used in healthcare.
